zoning.note: Two bands (access side / far side); each band is a row of columns stacking up to max_zones_per_column zones. Zone parts follow their spaces. Widths are catalog design minima. An optional through column (up to max_through_column zones stacked front to rear) runs the full depth at the left or right end, e.g. a living-dining great room from street to garden.

zoning.note_area_shift: Strategy B stepped: a column narrower than its minimum (zone minimum, driveway for the garage) is widened inside its band; the zones of that band trade area by at most max_area_shift. Anticipates the area assignment of step 9.

circulation.note: Circulation is a network, not a zone: the foyer takes the entry, halls are carved from the cells they serve, and paths through passable rooms consume a strip of the design width from those rooms. Private terminal rooms open only onto circulation (foyer or hall) or en-suite, from the bedroom to its bath or closet.

area_analysis.note: Step 6.6: area matrix per lot (program profile x vertical scheme x strategy). Evaluation stages: E0 area budget per floor, indices and containment; E1 measured site (access, paving, garden) with the simplest strategy that holds the footprint; E2 full zoning for the best one-floor cells only.
area_analysis.garden_min_note: Indicative threshold, not normative in RS-1-7: below it a cell is reported as 'fits with a small garden'.

frontage.note: Street-facing width the ground floor needs: garage lanes and entry are hard; the living-room street anchor is soft (it has a street-view fallback).

daily_use.note: Spaces used every day; their area off the entry floor is the stair dependency.

source.citation: Student-defined area-analysis hypothesis, spaceplan step 6.6 (2026-10); validate with pilot pre-approved plans and local practitioners

vertical_schemes.note: Vertical distribution schemes (step 6.6). A scheme assigns groups of spaces to floors; the household weighs the metrics, never excludes a scheme. Hard rules: a space with floor_preference 0 (mobility, garage) stays on the ground floor, and a cohesive group (a suite) moves with its pinned member so it is never split across floors; hosted spaces follow their host; circulation is split in proportion to each floor's net area; a stair is added on every floor of a two-floor scheme.

laundry_rule.note: Cultural aspect from step 6.5c: laundry near the bedrooms follows them upstairs; service-yard laundry stays with the kitchen.

schemes.note: Only when the lot has a view or is a hillside lot, and never with a reduced-mobility member (daily life would be upstairs).

scoring.note: Provisional indicator of a vertical scheme until the common quality score of step 6.8. Metrics in [0, 1]; household facts multiply weights; the trajectory takes the larger multiplier of the current and next stage. Open-area metric = open area (lot - footprint - paving - deck, the complement of the occupancy index) / (reference fraction x lot area), capped at 1; frontage metric = 0.5 + margin / (2 x margin scale), clipped; cost metric = 1 - relative index.

multipliers.note: Aging in place or reduced mobility of the primary couple: their daily life on the entry floor. A reduced-mobility relative is covered by the hard ground-floor rule of their suite.
Young children sleep on the parents' floor.
Teenagers or unrelated adults value vertical separation from the primary suite.
Children or a lawn-and-play patio raise the value of open area.
Temporary residents (often older relatives) need a ground-floor room.

source.citation: Student-defined area-analysis hypothesis, spaceplan step 6.6 (2026-10); validate with pilot pre-approved plans and local practitioners
